mainTopic: The end of the walled-cities discussion (קדושה ראשונה), and the opening אגדתא on מגילת אסתר: ויהי בימי, the traditions of רבי לוי, and the opening פסוקים of the חכמים
overview: This amud finishes a discussion about walled cities. The גמרא fixes the wording of a ברייתא: the returning exiles did not consecrate the cities, they only found them and listed them, because קדושה ראשונה lasts forever. That clashes with another view of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי. The גמרא answers that two תנאים reported him differently, or that the 'forever' view really belongs to רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי, based on 'אשר לוא חומה'. Then the גמרא turns to the מגילה itself. It tests the tradition that 'ויהי' signals trouble, and רב אשי narrows it to 'ויהי בימי'. Next come three traditions of רבי לוי: אמוץ and אמציה were brothers, which shows that ישעיהו descended from the modest תמר, and the ארון took up no space and stood by a miracle. The amud ends with a series of פסוקים that חכמים used to open the מגילה, including the lesson that ה׳ does not rejoice when the wicked fall but makes others rejoice. רב דימי בר יצחק's opening continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why would they need to consecrate the cities?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading that the exiles 'consecrated' the walled cities. The same ברייתא later says no new consecration is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא itself says later that there is no need to consecrate them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the wording of the ברייתא it just quoted. That wording said the returning exiles 'consecrated' these walled cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Later in the same ברייתא, the walled cities keep their status because the first קדושה lasts forever. If the holiness never went away, there was nothing to consecrate. So the ברייתא seems to contradict itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Now (used to mean: how can you say this, when...?)

phrases.english: Now, didn't they say
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is the corrected wording. It just means 'look, they said.'

phrases.english: it is not necessary to consecrate them!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא [הָא] אָמְרִי לָא צְרִיכָא לְקַדּוֹשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from the previous amud (10a) about the ברייתא listing walled cities.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording 'they consecrated them' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction. The ברייתא's own ending says the first holiness lasts forever, so no new consecration is possible or needed.

steps.title: They found the cities and listed them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the wording. The exiles did not consecrate the cities; they found them and counted them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it this way: they found these cities and listed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing how we read the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exiles' action was only identifying and recording which cities were walled from יהושע's time. That fits the idea that the original holiness was still there and needed no new act.

phrases.english: Rather: they found these and enumerated them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: מָצְאוּ אֶת אֵלּוּ וּמְנָאוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exiles performed a new consecration of the walled cities.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exiles only found and recorded cities that were already holy.

steps.title: Any city with a tradition of a wall from יהושע's time
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. The list is not limited to those cities: any city known by tradition to have been walled since יהושע keeps these laws, because קדושה ראשונה lasts forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only these cities. Any city that you know by family tradition was walled since the days of יהושע בן נון follows all these laws. This is because the first sanctification made the land holy for its own time and also for the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the ברייתא. It gives the general rule and the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The listed cities are only examples. The real test is a reliable tradition of a wall from יהושע's time. The reason is that the original קדושה from יהושע's conquest never ended, even after the exile.

keyTerms.meaning: The first sanctification of the land (in יהושע's time)

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether the first קדושה lasts forever is a major question. It affects walled-city laws (such as selling houses and when פורים is read) and many land-based מצוות.

phrases.english: And not only these,
phrases.notes: 'These' means the walled cities listed in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: but any city about which you receive a tradition
from your ancestors that it was surrounded by a wall
from the days of Joshua son of Nun —
all these מצוות apply in it,
because the first consecration sanctified it for its time
and sanctified it for the future.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא אֵלּוּ בִּלְבַד, אֶלָּא כׇּל שֶׁתַּעֲלֶה לְךָ מָסוֹרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the same ברייתא, now giving its general rule and reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any city with a tradition of a wall from יהושע's time keeps walled-city laws, because קדושה ראשונה קידשה לעתיד לבא.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל contradicts himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that this ברייתא clashes with another statement of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is difficult: one statement of רבי ישמעאל contradicts another statement of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction between two teachings attributed to the same תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבי ישמעאל says the first קדושה lasts forever. Earlier, on the previous amud (10a), his statement about the walled cities showed that he holds the first קדושה did not last. The same person cannot hold both views.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not רבי ישמעאל arguing with someone else. It is two reports of the SAME rabbi that seem to clash.

phrases.english: It is difficult: Rabbi Yishmael contradicts Rabbi Yishmael.
phrases.notes: The other statement is from the previous amud, where his view showed that the first holiness did not last.

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the reason given in step 3 to raise a contradiction with an earlier teaching.
steps.kashyaTarget: The attribution of 'קדושה ראשונה קידשה לעתיד לבא' to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Elsewhere the same תנא held that the first holiness was cancelled. He cannot hold both positions.

steps.title: Two תנאים reported his view differently
steps.stepSummary: First answer: two later תנאים disagree about what רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי actually held.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two תנאים disagree about what רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי held.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying the two statements come from two different reporters of רבי ישמעאל's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל himself did not contradict himself. Each version reflects how a different student transmitted his opinion. One reported 'forever' and the other reported 'cancelled.'

phrases.english: It is a dispute between two tanna'im
about the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּרֵי תַנָּאֵי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ישמעאל himself said two clashing things.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two later תנאים reported his opinion differently.

steps.title: The statement really belongs to רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the 'forever' statement was not said by רבי ישמעאל at all. It was said by his brother רבי אלעזר בר יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say that this statement was really said by רבי אלעזר בר יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way out. The statement was attributed to the wrong rabbi.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is then no contradiction inside רבי ישמעאל's view. He holds the first קדושה was cancelled. The view that it lasts forever belongs to רבי אלעזר. The next step brings a source showing that רבי אלעזר holds this.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: הָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר יוֹסֵי אַמְרַהּ,
phrases.english: this statement, Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei said it,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר יוֹסֵי אַמְרַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different answer to the contradiction in step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements belong to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'forever' statement belongs to רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי.

steps.title: Proof from 'אשר לוא חומה'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי holds that a city that once had a wall keeps its status even after the wall is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי said that the פסוק says 'אשר לוא חומה.' This teaches that even if the city has no wall now, it counts if it had one before.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source showing that רבי אלעזר really holds the 'forever' view, which supports the second answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word לוא is written like 'no' but read like 'it has.' So the פסוק hints at a city that has no wall now but did have one before. That city still counts as walled, which matches the idea that the original status lasts.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
'Which has a wall' (ויקרא כה:ל), written with an א

steps.whatToRemember: The contradiction about רבי ישמעאל has two answers. Either two תנאים reported him differently, or the 'forever' view really belongs to רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי, based on 'אשר לוא חומה.'

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אָמַר:
phrases.english: as it is taught: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said:
"Which has a wall,"
phrases.notes: Here לוא is spelled with an א, which means 'no,' but it is read as 'has.' Both meanings are used.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עַכְשָׁיו
phrases.english: even though it does not have a wall now
but it had one before.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the second answer (step 6) with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי holds the original walled status, and the first קדושה, continue

steps.title: 'ויהי' always signals trouble
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins explaining the מגילה. It quotes a tradition from אנשי כנסת הגדולה that the word 'ויהי' always signals sorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: The מגילה opens: 'ויהי בימי אחשורוש.' רבי לוי (some say רבי יונתן) said: We have a tradition from אנשי כנסת הגדולה that wherever it says 'ויהי,' it means trouble and grief.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the walled-city topic and starts a new section of explanations on the פסוקים of מגילת אסתר. It begins with the first word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ויהי is read as a hint to 'וי' (woe). So the opening of the מגילה already warns that a disaster is coming in אחשורוש's time. This tradition is said to go back to אנשי כנסת הגדולה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it was'; here read as a sign of woe
And some say (another rabbi said it)
The Men of the Great Assembly

steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a long series of explanations on the מגילה. The next part of the גמרא will test this rule against other פסוקים that use 'ויהי.'

phrases.english: "And it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus"
phrases.notes: This is the very first פסוק of מגילת אסתר.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Levi said, and some say it was Rabbi Yonatan:
This matter is a tradition in our hands
from the Men of the Great Assembly:
anywhere that "vayhi" is said,
it is nothing other than an expression of grief.
phrases.notes: Think of ויהי as sounding like 'וי' plus 'הי,' which both mean woe.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ״, אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a completely new topic: explanations on the פסוקים of the מגילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wherever the word ויהי appears, it signals trouble or grief.

steps.title: Proofs from אסתר, רות and בראשית that 'ויהי' signals trouble
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists פסוקים that open with 'וַיְהִי' and lead into trouble: המן, a famine, human wickedness before the מבול, the building of the city and tower at בבל, and the war of אמרפל.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And it was in the days of אחשורוש': there was המן. 'And it was in the days when the judges judged': there was a famine. 'And it was when man began to multiply': 'And ה׳ saw that man's wickedness was great.' 'And it was as they traveled from the east': 'Come, let us build ourselves a city.' 'And it was in the days of אמרפל': 'they made war.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the rule from the last step by showing several פסוקים where 'וַיְהִי' is followed by something bad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each example has two parts. First comes the 'וַיְהִי' opening. Then comes the trouble that follows it, sometimes in the same פסוק and sometimes a few פסוקים later. The pattern repeats, so the rule looks well supported.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it was' / 'and it came to pass'. Here it is treated as a sign of sorrow.
A king in the days of אברהם who waged war (בראשית יד)

phrases.english: "And it was in the days of Ahasuerus": there was Haman.
phrases.notes: This is the very first פסוק of the מגילה, which is why the גמרא starts with it.

phrases.english: "And it was in the days when the judges judged": there was a famine.
phrases.notes: This is the opening of מגילת רות.

phrases.english: "And it was when man began to multiply":
"And the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great."
phrases.notes: This leads up to the מבול.

phrases.english: "And it was as they traveled from the east":
"Come, let us build ourselves a city."
phrases.notes: This is the story of the tower of בבל.

phrases.english: "And it was in the days of Amraphel": "they made war."

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ הֲוָה הָמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule from step 8 that 'וַיְהִי' signals sorrow.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that 'וַיְהִי' always signals sorrow.
steps.raayaSupportSource: פסוקים from אסתר, רות and בראשית where 'וַיְהִי' leads into trouble.

steps.title: More proofs from יהושע and שמואל that 'ויהי' signals trouble
steps.stepSummary: The list continues with examples from נביאים: the sword-bearing figure יהושע met near יריחו, the sin of מעילה, חנה's childlessness, שמואל's sons, שאול's jealousy of דוד, and דוד being told he would not build the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And it was when יהושע was by יריחו': 'his sword drawn in his hand.' 'And ה׳ was with יהושע': 'and the children of Israel trespassed.' 'And there was a man from רמתים': 'for he loved חנה, but ה׳ had closed her womb.' 'And it was when שמואל grew old': 'his sons did not walk in his ways.' 'And דוד was successful in all his ways': 'and שאול eyed דוד with suspicion.' 'And it was when the king sat in his house': 'only you will not build the House.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps adding examples, now from the books of יהושע and שמואל, where 'וַיְהִי' leads into something painful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some of these examples open with good news. ה׳ was with יהושע, and דוד was successful. Even so, the 'וַיְהִי' is tied to trouble nearby. This shows that the rule holds even when the opening words sound positive.

keyTerms.meaning: Closed her womb, meaning she could not have children

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא brings a long chain of 'וַיְהִי' פסוקים, each linked to trouble. This builds strong support for the rule of אנשי כנסת הגדולה.

phrases.english: "And it was when Joshua was by Jericho":
"and his sword drawn in his hand."
phrases.notes: This describes the figure יהושע saw standing before him with a drawn sword. It was a frightening sight.

phrases.english: "And the Lord was with Joshua":
"And the children of Israel trespassed."
phrases.notes: This is the sin of עכן, who took from the spoils of יריחו.

phrases.english: "And there was a certain man from Ramathaim":
phrases.notes: This is אלקנה, חנה's husband.

phrases.aramaic: ״כִּי אֶת חַנָּה אָהֵב וַה׳ סָגַר רַחְמָהּ״.
phrases.english: "For he loved Hannah, but the Lord had closed her womb."
"And it was when Samuel grew old":
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The פסוק itself says 'כַּאֲשֶׁר'. Either way it means 'when'.

phrases.english: "And his sons did not walk in his ways."
"And David was successful in all his ways [and the Lord was with him]":
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording. They finish the פסוק so you can see the whole thing.

phrases.english: "And Saul eyed David with suspicion."
"And it was when the king sat in his house":
phrases.notes: This is דוד, who then wanted to build a house for ה׳.

phrases.english: "Only you shall not build the House."
phrases.notes: דוד was told that his son would build the בית המקדש instead of him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיְהִי בִּהְיוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּירִיחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list of proofs from step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that 'וַיְהִי' always signals sorrow.
steps.raayaSupportSource: פסוקים from יהושע and שמואל (and the related פסוק about building the בית המקדש).

steps.title: Challenge from the joyful eighth day of the משכן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule. 'וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי' introduces the day the משכן was dedicated. A ברייתא says that day brought joy before ה׳ like the day of creation, and it learns this from the shared word 'וַיְהִי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written, 'And it was on the eighth day.' And a ברייתא teaches: on that day there was joy before the Holy One, Blessed be He, like the day heaven and earth were created. It is written here, 'And it was on the eighth day,' and it is written there, 'And it was one day'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the rule. Here is a 'וַיְהִי' that introduces a day of great happiness, not sorrow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge has two parts. First comes a 'וַיְהִי' פסוק about the משכן. Then comes a ברייתא that calls that day joyful, comparing it to creation through the matching word 'וַיְהִי'. If 'וַיְהִי' can be connected to joy, then it cannot always mean sorrow.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? This phrase opens a challenge from a פסוק.
It is written here, and it is written there. This compares two פסוקים through a shared word.

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא uses the word 'וַיְהִי' itself to prove joy, by linking it to creation. So this is not just a happy story that happens to start with 'וַיְהִי'. The very word is being used as a sign of joy.

phrases.english: But isn't it written: "And it was on the eighth day"?
phrases.notes: This is the day the משכן was dedicated, after the seven days of preparation.

phrases.english: And it is taught: on that day there was joy
before the Holy One, Blessed be He,
like the day on which heaven and earth were created.
It is written here: "And it was on the eighth day,"
and it is written there: "And it was [morning], one day"!
phrases.notes: This is from the first day of creation, where the full פסוק says 'וַיְהִי עֶרֶב וַיְהִי בֹקֶר יוֹם אֶחָד'. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָכְתִיב וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the list of proofs, the גמרא challenges the rule they supported.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of אנשי כנסת הגדולה that every 'וַיְהִי' signals sorrow.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי' introduces a day of joy, and a ברייתא even uses the word 'וַיְהִי' to compare it to the joy of creation. So 'וַיְהִי' does not always signal sorrow.

steps.title: The dedication day also had a tragedy
steps.stepSummary: The rule survives: the day the משכן was dedicated was joyful, but נדב and אביהוא died on that same day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even that day had sorrow, because נדב and אביהוא died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 11. The joyful 'וַיְהִי' of the משכן's dedication day still led to sorrow, because נדב and אביהוא died that day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge said that 'וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי' introduced pure joy. The answer is that the day held both: joy before ה׳, and also the death of אהרן's two sons. So the rule that 'וַיְהִי' signals sorrow still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: The two sons of אהרן who died on the day the משכן was dedicated

phrases.english: Here, Nadav and Avihu died.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא שְׁכֵיב נָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from step 11 and defends the rule from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the event: the day contained sorrow as well as joy.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The day the משכן was dedicated was purely joyful, so 'וַיְהִי' there did not signal sorrow.
steps.terutzMaskana: That day also brought the death of נדב and אביהוא, so 'וַיְהִי' still introduces sorrow.

steps.title: Many more happy uses of 'וַיְהִי'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists more פסוקים where 'וַיְהִי' leads to good or neutral events: the building of the בית המקדש, יעקב seeing רחל, and the days of creation.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it says 'וַיְהִי' about the 480th year, when the בית המקדש was built. It says 'וַיְהִי' when יעקב saw רחל. It says 'וַיְהִי' about the evening and morning of the first day, and also the second day and the third day. There are many more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rule again, this time with a whole stream of examples. In none of them does 'וַיְהִי' lead to sorrow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer about נדב and אביהוא worked for one פסוק. Here there are too many happy examples to explain away one by one. The closing word 'טוּבָא' ("many") shows that the simple rule cannot stand as stated.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכְתִיב: ״וַיְהִי בִשְׁמוֹנִים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה״!
phrases.english: But isn't it written: "And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year"!
phrases.notes: This פסוק in מלכים begins the story of שלמה building the בית המקדש. That was a happy event.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכְתִיב: ״וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָה יַעֲקֹב אֶת רָחֵל״!
phrases.english: And isn't it written: "And it came to pass when Jacob saw Rachel"!

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכְתִיב ״וַיְהִי עֶרֶב וַיְהִי בֹקֶר יוֹם אֶחָד״!
phrases.english: And isn't it written: "And it was evening and it was morning, one day"!
And isn't there the second! And isn't there the third!
phrases.notes: He means the second and third days of creation, which also say 'וַיְהִי'.

phrases.english: And aren't there many!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָכְתִיב: ״וַיְהִי בִשְׁמוֹנִים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 12 rescued the rule for one פסוק, the גמרא brings many more counter-examples.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule from step 8 that 'וַיְהִי' always signals sorrow.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Many פסוקים use 'וַיְהִי' for happy or neutral events, so the word cannot always mean sorrow.

steps.title: רב אשי narrows the rule to 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says a plain 'וַיְהִי' can go either way. The phrase 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' always signals sorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: a plain 'וַיְהִי' sometimes means sorrow and sometimes does not. But 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' ("and it came to pass in the days of") always means sorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי resolves the challenge by narrowing the rule. The sorrow-signal applies to the full phrase 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי', not to every 'וַיְהִי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The happy examples from step 13 show that plain 'וַיְהִי' is not a reliable sign. רב אשי keeps a firm rule, but limits it to one specific phrase. None of the happy examples in step 13 use that phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: There is this way and there is that way (it can go either way)
And it came to pass in the days of

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי does not say plain 'וַיְהִי' never signals sorrow. He says it can go either way. Only the phrase 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' is a guaranteed sign of sorrow.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the final form of the rule used to explain the opening words of the מגילה: 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ'.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Every "vayhi": there is this way and there is that way,
phrases.notes: Meaning: a plain 'וַיְהִי' sometimes leads to sorrow and sometimes to good things.

phrases.english: "Vayhi bimei" is nothing other than an expression of sorrow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: כׇּל ״וַיְהִי״ — אִיכָּא הָכִי וְאִיכָּא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the large קשיא of step 13 by narrowing the rule from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to a more specific phrase.
steps.terutzMaskana: Plain 'וַיְהִי' can go either way. Only 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' always signals sorrow.

steps.title: The five places that say 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists the five פסוקים that open with 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי'. All of them lead into sorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are five places that say 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי': in the days of אחשורוש, in the days when the judges judged, in the days of אמרפל, in the days of אחז, and in the days of יהויקים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רב אשי's rule by listing every place the phrase 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' appears. Each one introduces a time of trouble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list is complete: there are exactly five such פסוקים, so the rule can be checked against all of them. The first one is the opening of the מגילה, which ties the rule back to the story of המן.

keyTerms.meaning: When the judges judged (the opening of מגילת רות)
A king of יהודה near the end of the first בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: Final rule: a plain 'וַיְהִי' can go either way, but 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' always signals sorrow. The מגילה opens with 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ', so trouble is coming.

phrases.english: There are five instances of "vayhi bimei":
"And it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus",
phrases.notes: This is the opening of the מגילה, leading to המן's plot.

phrases.english: "And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged",
phrases.notes: This is the start of מגילת רות, where a famine follows. Step 9 mentioned that famine.

phrases.english: "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel",
phrases.notes: This is the war of the kings in בראשית, mentioned back in step 9.

phrases.english: "And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz",
"And it came to pass in the days of Jehoiakim".

steps.triggerLanguage: חַמְשָׁה ״וַיְהִי בִּימֵי״ הָווּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב אשי's rule from step 14 by listing every case of 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי'.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's rule that 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי' always signals sorrow.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The five פסוקים in תנ"ך that open with 'וַיְהִי בִּימֵי', each of which introduces a time of trouble.

steps.title: רבי לוי's tradition: אמוץ and אמציה were brothers
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי passes down a tradition that אמוץ and אמציה were brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי לוי said: We have this as a tradition from our ancestors: אמוץ and אמציה were brothers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another tradition from רבי לוי: אמוץ, the father of the prophet ישעיהו, was the brother of אמציה, a king of יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a fact passed down from earlier generations, not something learned from a פסוק. On its own it looks like plain family history, so the גמרא will ask why it matters.

keyTerms.meaning: A tradition we hold, passed down by word of mouth
A king of יהודה from the family of דוד

phrases.english: And Rabbi Levi said:
This matter is a tradition in our hands from our ancestors:
Amoz and Amaziah were brothers.
phrases.notes: אמוץ is ישעיהו's father. אמציה was a king of יהודה, so he came from דוד's family.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי, דָּבָר זֶה מָסוֹרֶת בְּיָדֵינוּ מֵאֲבוֹתֵינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ויהי בימי discussion to another tradition of רבי לוי.

steps.title: What does this tradition teach us?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it matters that אמוץ and אמציה were brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this teaching us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what new lesson comes from knowing that these two men were brothers. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not an attack on רבי לוי. The גמרא simply wants to know what the tradition adds, since a family fact alone does not seem important.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it teaching us? The גמרא's way of asking for the point of a statement

phrases.english: What is this teaching us?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the purpose of רבי לוי's tradition.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson comes from the fact that אמוץ and אמציה were brothers?

steps.title: A modest bride merits kings and prophets
steps.stepSummary: The answer begins with רבי יונתן's teaching that a כלה who is modest in her father-in-law's house will have kings and prophets among her descendants.
steps.simpleTranslation: It fits what רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Any כלה who is modest in her father-in-law's house merits that kings and prophets come from her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts its answer by quoting a teaching about the reward for modesty. It will later connect this teaching back to רבי לוי's tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer comes in stages. First comes the rule: modesty brings descendants who are kings and prophets. Next the גמרא will show where the rule comes from. Then it will show how רבי לוי's tradition supplies the 'prophets' part.

keyTerms.meaning: A bride or young married woman
She merits, earns as a reward

phrases.english: It is like that which was said by

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, who said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל כַּלָּה שֶׁהִיא צְנוּעָה בְּבֵית חָמִיהָ
phrases.english: Any bride who is modest in the house of her father-in-law
merits that kings and prophets come out from her.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי לוי's tradition helps support רבי יונתן's teaching that a modest כלה merits kings and prophets.

steps.title: The source is תמר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source and brings the פסוק about יהודה and תמר.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this? From תמר, as it says: "יהודה saw her and thought she was a harlot, because she had covered her face."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי יונתן's rule comes from and points to the story of תמר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says יהודה thought תמר was a harlot "because she covered her face." The גמרא will now show that this wording, read literally, does not make sense, and that the strange wording hides the lesson about modesty.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.english: From where do we know this? From Tamar,
as it is written: "Judah saw her
and thought her to be a harlot, for she had covered her face."
phrases.notes: This פסוק is from בראשית, chapter 38.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָלַן? מִתָּמָר, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the rule in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a modest כלה merits kings and prophets
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 38:15, the story of יהודה and תמר

steps.title: Covering the face does not make someone look like a harlot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how covering her face could make יהודה think תמר was a harlot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because she covered her face, he thought she was a harlot?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the simple reading of the פסוק makes no sense. This sets up the new reading in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A harlot usually shows her face. She does not cover it. So covering her face cannot be the reason יהודה thought she was a harlot, and the פסוק must mean something else.

phrases.english: Because she covered her face
"he thought her to be a harlot"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּכִסְּתָה פָּנֶיהָ וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לְזוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the simple reading of the פסוק just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The literal meaning of "כי כסתה פניה"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Covering the face is the opposite of how a harlot acts, so it cannot be the reason he thought she was one.

steps.title: She was always covered at home, so יהודה did not recognize her
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק means that תמר always covered her face in יהודה's home, so he did not know what she looked like.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, because she used to cover her face in her father-in-law's house, he did not know what she looked like. She earned a reward, and kings and prophets came from her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads the פסוק. תמר's covered face was her habit at home, and that is why יהודה did not recognize her on the road.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "because she covered her face" now explain why he did not recognize her. They are not the reason he thought she was a harlot. Her modesty in her father-in-law's house earned her descendants who were kings and prophets, which proves רבי יונתן's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And he did not know her (her face)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דְּכִסְּתָה פָּנֶיהָ בְּבֵית חָמִיהָ,
phrases.english: Rather, because she covered her face in the house of her father-in-law,
and he did not know her,
she merited, and kings and prophets came out from her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דְּכִסְּתָה פָּנֶיהָ בְּבֵית חָמִיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 with a new reading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The covered face was the reason he thought she was a harlot.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her habit of covering her face at home is why he did not recognize her, and that modesty earned her royal and prophetic descendants.

steps.title: Kings through דוד, prophets through ישעיהו
steps.stepSummary: Kings came from תמר through דוד. Prophets came from her through ישעיהו, whose father אמוץ was the brother of king אמציה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Kings came from דוד. Prophets came through what רבי לוי said: we have a tradition that אמוץ and אמציה were brothers, and the פסוק says "The vision of ישעיהו son of אמוץ."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how both parts of the reward came true, and this finally explains why רבי לוי's tradition matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד came from תמר's son פרץ, so the kings are clear. The prophets are not stated in any פסוק. רבי לוי's tradition fills that gap: אמוץ was the brother of king אמציה, so he too came from דוד's family, which makes his son ישעיהו a descendant of תמר.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי לוי's family tradition is the link that proves prophets descended from תמר, as a reward for her modesty.
steps.confusionAlert: There are two different people here: אמוץ, the father of ישעיהו, and the prophet עמוס, whose name sounds similar in English. Only אמוץ is meant.

phrases.english: Kings — from David,
prophets — as Rabbi Levi said,
A tradition in our hands from our ancestors:
Amoz and Amaziah were brothers,
and it is written: "The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz."

steps.triggerLanguage: מְלָכִים מִדָּוִד, נְבִיאִים דְּאָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof by showing both kings and prophets came from תמר, which answers step 17.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי לוי's tradition together with ישעיהו 1:1
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי לוי's tradition teaches that ישעיהו came from דוד's line and so from תמר.

steps.title: The space of the ארון is not part of the measurement
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי gives another tradition: the place of the ארון does not take up any measured space.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי לוי said: We have this as a tradition from our ancestors: the place of the ארון is not part of the measurement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new tradition from רבי לוי about the ארון in the קדש הקדשים. This opens a new topic that the גמרא will go on to explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that when the room holding the ארון was measured, the ארון itself did not use up any of that space. This is a new and surprising claim, unrelated to the תמר discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the ארון stood
Is not counted in the measurement

phrases.english: And Rabbi Levi said:
This matter is a tradition in our hands from our ancestors:
The place of the Ark is not part of the measurement.
phrases.notes: He means the room around the ארון, the קדש הקדשים. The ארון's own space wasn't counted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי, דָּבָר זֶה מָסוֹרֶת בְּיָדֵינוּ מֵאֲבוֹתֵינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new tradition of רבי לוי after the תמר discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The space of the ארון is not counted in the measurement of its room.

steps.title: A ברייתא and two פסוקים about the space around the ארון
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רבי לוי: the ארון had ten אמות of space on every side. The פסוקים show the room was twenty אמות long and the כרובים' wings filled all twenty.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches the same thing as רבי לוי: the ארון that משה made had ten אמות of empty space on each side. The פסוק says the inner room was twenty אמות long. Another פסוק says each כרוב's wing was ten אמות, so the two wings together filled all twenty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא and two פסוקים to back up רבי לוי's tradition that the ארון took up no space. This step lays out the numbers, and the next step draws the conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ten אמות on one side plus ten on the other already adds up to twenty. The whole room was only twenty אמות long, and the כרובים' wings also covered exactly twenty. So the numbers leave no room for the ארון's own width.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא. This brings support for what was just said.
Cubit or cubits, a unit of length
The inner sanctuary, the קדש הקדשים
A כרוב, one of the winged golden figures above the ארון

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
The ark that Moshe made

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לוֹ עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת לְכׇל רוּחַ,
phrases.english: had ten cubits on every side,
phrases.notes: This means ten cubits of empty space between the ארון and each wall.

phrases.english: And it is written: "And before the Sanctuary
twenty cubits in length,"
phrases.notes: This is the קדש הקדשים, the room where the ארון stood. The whole room was only twenty cubits long.

phrases.english: And it is written: "The wing of the one cherub was ten cubits
and the wing of the other cherub was ten cubits,"

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא and פסוקים to support רבי לוי's tradition from step 23
steps.raayaObject: רבי לוי's claim that the place of the ארון did not take up measured space
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about ten אמות on each side, plus the פסוקים about the twenty-אמה דביר and the ten-אמה wings of the כרובים

steps.title: The ארון stood by a miracle
steps.stepSummary: Since the measurements leave no room for the ארון, the גמרא concludes that it stood there by a miracle.
steps.simpleTranslation: So where was the ארון itself standing? We must learn from this that it stood by a miracle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion from the numbers in the previous step. The ארון must have stood there miraculously, taking up no space at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'where was the ארון standing?' is not a real question. It points out that the numbers leave no room for the ארון. The only way to explain this is a נס, which confirms רבי לוי's tradition.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, must we not learn from this? A formula for drawing a conclusion

steps.whatToRemember: The קדש הקדשים was twenty אמות long and the ארון had ten אמות on each side. So the ארון itself took up no space; it stood there by a miracle.

phrases.english: The ark itself, where was it standing?
Rather, must one not learn from this:
it stood by means of a miracle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָרוֹן גּוּפֵיהּ הֵיכָא הֲוָה קָאֵי? אֶלָּא לָאו שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the measurements in step 24
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ארון took up no physical space; it stood in the קדש הקדשים by a miracle.

steps.title: רבי יונתן opens the מגילה with a פסוק about cutting off בבל
steps.stepSummary: A new section begins. רבי יונתן introduces מגילת אסתר with a פסוק in ישעיהו where ה׳ promises to cut off from בבל its name, remnant, offspring and posterity.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן began his teaching of this section, the מגילה, with this פסוק: 'I will rise up against them... and I will cut off from בבל name and remnant, offspring and posterity, says ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: opening lines that חכמים used to introduce the study of the מגילה. This step quotes רבי יונתן's פסוק, and the next step explains it word by word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פתיחתא is an introduction that connects a פסוק from elsewhere in תנ״ך to the topic being taught. Here the פסוק promises the full destruction of בבל. רבי יונתן links it to the story of the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: He opened it with an opening, meaning he introduced the topic with a פסוק
Section or passage; here, מגילת אסתר

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan opened for it an introduction
phrases.notes: He started his teaching of the מגילה with a פסוק from somewhere else that hints to the story.

phrases.english: to this passage from here:
phrases.notes: This passage means מגילת אסתר.

phrases.english: "And I will rise up against them, etc.,
phrases.notes: The word "etc." means the פסוק goes on. It is from ישעיהו.

phrases.english: and I will cut off from Babylonia name and remnant
and offspring and posterity, says the Lord."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of opening teachings to the מגילה, unrelated to the ארון discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יונתן introduces the מגילה with ישעיהו's prophecy about cutting off בבל.

steps.title: Reading each word of the פסוק, ending with ושתי
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן explains each word: name is their writing, remnant is their language, offspring is their kingdom, and posterity is ושתי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Name' is their writing. 'Remnant' is their language. 'Offspring' is their kingdom. 'Posterity' is ושתי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן explains each of the four words in the פסוק. The last word ties the פסוק to the מגילה, because it refers to ושתי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word stands for something of בבל that would be wiped out: its writing, its language and its kingdom. The last word, נכד, can also mean grandchild. It points to ושתי, a descendant of the kings of בבל, whose removal opens the story of the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: ושתי, the queen removed at the start of the מגילה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read נכד here as a general word for future generations. רבי יונתן reads it as pointing to one specific person, ושתי.

phrases.english: "Name" — this is the writing,
"Remnant" — this is the language,
"Offspring" — this is the kingdom,
"And posterity" — this is Vashti.
phrases.notes: The word נכד can also mean grandchild, and ושתי came from the royal family of בבל.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שֵׁם״ — זֶה הַכְּתָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the words of the פסוק quoted in step 26
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four words name, remnant, offspring and posterity stand for בבל's writing, language, kingdom, and ושתי.

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני opens with thorns replaced by good trees
steps.stepSummary: A second opening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני introduces the מגילה with the פסוק 'Instead of the thorn the cypress shall come up, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall come up.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני began his teaching of the מגילה with this פסוק: 'Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress, and instead of the nettle shall come up the myrtle.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second חכם's opening to the מגילה. This step only quotes the פסוק, and the following steps explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes bad, prickly plants being replaced by good, pleasant ones. רבי שמואל בר נחמני will read it as the wicked people of the מגילה being replaced by righteous ones.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי, פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani opened for it an introduction
to this passage from here:
"Instead of the thorn shall the cypress come up,
and instead of the nettle shall the myrtle come up."
phrases.notes: Keep the myrtle in mind; הדס is also a name of אסתר.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי, פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different opening to the מגילה, parallel to רבי יונתן's in step 26
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמואל בר נחמני introduces the מגילה with ישעיהו's image of thorns replaced by cypress and myrtle.

steps.title: The thorn is המן, who made himself an idol
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני explains that 'instead of the thorn' means instead of המן הרשע, who turned himself into an object of עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Instead of the thorn' means instead of the wicked המן, who made himself into an idol.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני starts explaining his פסוק piece by piece, beginning with the thorn, which he says is המן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: המן demanded that everyone bow down to him, so he made himself like an idol. Calling him a thorn connects to עבודה זרה. The next step brings a פסוק showing that the word 'thorns' is linked to idol worship.

keyTerms.meaning: Idol worship, or an object of idol worship

phrases.english: "Instead of the thorn" — instead of the wicked Haman,
who made himself into an object of idol worship,

steps.triggerLanguage: ״תַּחַת הַנַּעֲצוּץ״ — תַּחַת הָמָן הָרָשָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the פסוק from step 28
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'thorn' in the פסוק refers to המן, who made himself an object of עבודה זרה.

steps.title: A פסוק linking thorns to idol worship
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves that the word 'thorn' is tied to עבודה זרה from a פסוק that mentions 'all the thorns and all the brambles.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And upon all the thorns and upon all the brambles.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק as proof that the word נעצוץ, thorn, is used for עבודה זרה. This explains why המן is called a thorn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word, נעצוצים, appears in another פסוק in ישעיהו, which is understood as speaking about idol worship. Since that word is linked to עבודה זרה, it fits המן, who made himself an idol.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written; this introduces a proof from a פסוק

phrases.english: as it is written: "And upon all thorns,
phrases.notes: This is another פסוק in ישעיהו using the same word for thorns, understood as talking about idol worship.

phrases.english: and upon all brambles."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וּבְכֹל הַנַּעֲצוּצִים וּבְכֹל הַנַּהֲלוֹלִים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 29's claim that 'thorn' hints to עבודה זרה
steps.raayaObject: The link between the word נעצוץ (thorn) and עבודה זרה, which explains why המן is called a thorn
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in ישעיהו: 'And upon all thorns and upon all brambles'

steps.title: The cypress is מרדכי
steps.stepSummary: The 'cypress' (בְּרוֹשׁ) that grows in place of the thorn is מרדכי, who is called the 'head' (רֹאשׁ) of all spices.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The cypress shall come up' means מרדכי, who is called the head of all the spices.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני keeps reading the פסוק. The cypress that replaces the thorn (המן) is מרדכי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בְּרוֹשׁ has the word רֹאשׁ (head) inside it. So the cypress stands for someone called a 'head', and the גמרא says that is מרדכי. The proof for this nickname comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Cypress tree; it contains the sound רֹאשׁ, 'head'
מרדכי, the hero of the מגילה

phrases.english: "Shall the cypress come up"
this is Mordechai
who is called the head of all the spices,
phrases.notes: Listen for the word רֹאשׁ hiding inside בְּרוֹשׁ. That is the link.

steps.triggerLanguage: יַעֲלֶה בְּרוֹשׁ זֶה מָרְדֳּכַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the thorn (המן) to what replaces it (מרדכי).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cypress in the פסוק is מרדכי, the 'head' of spices.

steps.title: Proof that מרדכי is the head of spices
steps.stepSummary: The תורה lists 'head spices, pure myrrh' (מר דרור), and the Aramaic translation of that is 'מר דכי', which sounds like מרדכי.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Take for yourself head spices, pure myrrh.' We translate 'pure myrrh' into Aramaic as 'מר דכי'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves why מרדכי is called the head of spices. It uses a פסוק about the spices for the anointing oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls pure myrrh one of the 'head' spices. Its Aramaic name, מר דכי, sounds just like מרדכי. So מרדכי is linked to the 'head' spice, and that ties back to the רֹאשׁ inside בְּרוֹשׁ.

keyTerms.meaning: Pure myrrh, one of the spices of the anointing oil
Aramaic for 'pure myrrh'; it sounds like מרדכי

phrases.english: as it is said: "And you, take for yourself
phrases.notes: This פסוק is in שמות, where ה׳ tells משה what spices go into the anointing oil.

phrases.english: head spices, pure myrrh",
and we translate it: "mor dechei."
phrases.notes: Say מֹר דְּכֵי quickly and you hear מרדכי. That is the whole point.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְאַתָּה קַח לְךָ בְּשָׂמִים רֹאשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the claim in step 31 that מרדכי is called the head of spices.
steps.raayaObject: That מרדכי is called the 'head' of spices.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות ל:כג, 'בשמים ראש מר דרור', and its Aramaic translation 'מר דכי'.

steps.title: The nettle is ושתי
steps.stepSummary: The 'nettle' (סִרְפַּד) is ושתי, granddaughter of נבוכדנצר, who burned (שָׂרַף) the covering (רְפִידַת) of the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Instead of the nettle' means instead of the wicked ושתי, granddaughter of the wicked נבוכדנצר, who burned the covering of the House of ה׳.
steps.whatsHappening: The next part of the פסוק is explained. The nettle that gets replaced is ושתי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word סִרְפַּד is read as two words joined together: שָׂרַף (burned) and רְפִידָה (covering). ושתי gets this name because her grandfather נבוכדנצר burned the בית המקדש. The proof that רְפִידָה means part of the בית המקדש comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Nettle, a stinging weed; read here as שָׂרַף + רְפִידָה
ושתי, the wicked queen before אסתר
נבוכדנצר, the Babylonian king who destroyed the first בית המקדש
Covering or upper part, here of the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for ושתי in the word itself. The link is through her grandfather's crime: סִרְפַּד = שָׂרַף רְפִידַת, 'burned the covering'.

phrases.english: "Instead of the nettle"
instead of the wicked Vashti
the daughter of the son of the wicked Nebuchadnezzar
who burned the covering of the House of ה׳,
phrases.notes: Put שָׂרַף and רְפִידַת together and you get the sounds of סִרְפַּד.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּחַת הַסִּרְפַּד תַּחַת וַשְׁתִּי הָרְשָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the second half of the פסוק, the nettle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The nettle is ושתי, named for her grandfather burning the בית המקדש.

steps.title: Proof that רפידה means part of the בית המקדש
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק in שיר השירים says 'its covering was gold', which shows that רְפִידָה is a part of the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Its covering was gold.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a short פסוק to show that the word רְפִידָה is used for the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wordplay in step 33 needs רְפִידָה to mean part of the House of ה׳. The פסוק 'רפידתו זהב' uses that word for a golden covering, which is read as the בית המקדש. That confirms the reading of סִרְפַּד.

phrases.english: as it is written: "Its covering was gold."
phrases.notes: This is from שיר השירים, describing a golden structure that the גמרא reads as the בית המקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב רְפִידָתוֹ זָהָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the meaning of רְפִידָה used in step 33.
steps.raayaObject: That רְפִידָה refers to part of the בית המקדש.

steps.title: The myrtle is אסתר
steps.stepSummary: The 'myrtle' (הֲדַס) that grows in place of the nettle is אסתר, who was also called הדסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The myrtle shall come up' means the righteous אסתר, who was called הדסה.
steps.whatsHappening: The next part of the פסוק is explained. The myrtle that replaces ושתי is אסתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This match is the most direct. הֲדַס (myrtle) is almost the same word as הֲדַסָּה, אסתר's other name. So just as אסתר replaced ושתי as queen, the myrtle replaces the nettle.

phrases.english: "Shall the myrtle come up"
this is the righteous Esther
who was called Hadassah,

steps.triggerLanguage: יַעֲלֶה הֲדַס זוֹ אֶסְתֵּר הַצַּדֶּקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives what replaces the nettle (ושתי): the myrtle (אסתר).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The myrtle in the פסוק is אסתר, called הדסה.

steps.title: Proof that אסתר was called הדסה
steps.stepSummary: The מגילה itself says מרדכי raised 'הדסה', which shows that אסתר had that name.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is said: 'And he raised הדסה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves from the מגילה that אסתר was called הדסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in the מגילה says מרדכי raised הדסה, 'that is אסתר'. This confirms the name, so the myrtle (הֲדַס) clearly points to her.

phrases.english: as it is said: "And he raised Hadassah."
phrases.notes: This is from the מגילה itself. The פסוק goes on to say 'that is אסתר'.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיְהִי אוֹמֵן אֶת הֲדַסָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the name הדסה used in step 35.

steps.title: The end of the verse: reading the מגילה and the days of פורים
steps.stepSummary: 'For a name to ה׳' is the reading of the מגילה, and 'an everlasting sign that will not be cut off' is the days of פורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And it shall be for ה׳ for a name' means the reading of the מגילה. 'For an everlasting sign that will not be cut off' means the days of פורים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני finishes the פסוק. Its last words describe the lasting results of the miracle: reading the מגילה and keeping פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After matching the people (המן, מרדכי, ושתי, אסתר), the end of the פסוק is read as what remains forever. Reading the מגילה makes ה׳'s 'name' known, and the days of פורים are a sign that will never stop.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמואל בר נחמני's whole פסוק is the פורים story: thorn = המן, cypress = מרדכי, nettle = ושתי, myrtle = אסתר, 'a name' = reading the מגילה, 'everlasting sign' = the days of פורים.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the reading of the מגילה and the holiday of פורים are pictured as lasting forever, already hinted at in the נביא.

phrases.english: "And it shall be for ה׳ for a name"
this is the reading of the Megillah.
"For an everlasting sign that will not be cut off"
these are the days of Purim.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָיָה לַה׳ לְשֵׁם זוֹ מִקְרָא מְגִילָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reading of the פסוק that began in step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The end of the פסוק refers to the reading of the מגילה and the days of פורים.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי's opening: ה׳ rejoices to do harm
steps.stepSummary: A new פתיחתא: רבי יהושע בן לוי opens the מגילה with a פסוק from דברים saying that just as ה׳ rejoiced to do good, so He will 'rejoice' to do harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי opened this section with an opening from here: 'And just as ה׳ rejoiced over you to do you good, so He will rejoice to harm you.'
steps.whatsHappening: A third opening to the מגילה begins. רבי יהושע בן לוי quotes a פסוק from the curses in דברים, and the גמרא will discuss it next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the last opening, which was about salvation, this פסוק speaks about punishment. It raises a hard idea: that ה׳ would 'rejoice' in harm. The פסוק is quoted with the middle cut out, and the discussion comes in the following steps.

keyTerms.meaning: An early אמורא from ארץ ישראל
An opening; a פסוק used to introduce a section

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi

phrases.aramaic: פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: opened an opening for this section from here:
"And it will be, just as ה׳ rejoiced over you

phrases.aramaic: לְהֵיטִיב אֶתְכֶם כֵּן יָשִׂישׂ... לְהָרַע אֶתְכֶם״.
phrases.english: to do you good, so He will rejoice... to harm you."
phrases.notes: The dots mean the גמרא skipped some middle words of the פסוק. It is from the curses in דברים.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, separate opening to the מגילה after רבי שמואל בר נחמני's opening ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע בן לוי introduces the מגילה with דברים כח:סג, about ה׳ rejoicing to do harm.

steps.title: Does ה׳ really rejoice when the wicked fall?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea from step 38 that ה׳ 'rejoices' to do harm. רבי יוחנן taught that ה׳ does not rejoice over the downfall of the wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does ה׳ really rejoice when the wicked fall? But a פסוק says that before the army they sang 'Give thanks to ה׳, for His kindness is forever,' and רבי יוחנן said the words 'for He is good' were left out because ה׳ does not rejoice when the wicked fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the פסוק from step 38 ('so ה׳ will rejoice' to destroy). It brings רבי יוחנן's teaching that ה׳ does NOT rejoice when the wicked fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual thanksgiving is 'Give thanks to ה׳, for He is good, for His kindness is forever.' At יהושפט's battle the words 'for He is good' were dropped, and רבי יוחנן explains that this is because the enemy was being destroyed. That clashes with reading the פסוק in דברים as saying ה׳ rejoices over harm.

keyTerms.meaning: And does He really rejoice? (an opening that sets up a challenge)

phrases.english: And does the Holy One, Blessed be He, rejoice
over the downfall of the wicked?
phrases.notes: This goes back to step 38, where ה׳ 'rejoices' to bring harm.

phrases.english: But it is written:
"As they went out before the army,
phrases.notes: This is from דברי הימים, when יהושפט's singers marched ahead of the army into battle.

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹמְרִים הוֹדוּ לַה׳ כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ״,
phrases.english: and they say: Give thanks to ה׳, for His kindness is forever,"
and רבי יוחנן said:

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא נֶאֱמַר ״כִּי טוֹב״ בְּהוֹדָאָה זוֹ?
phrases.english: Why was "for He is good" not said in this thanksgiving?

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שָׂמֵחַ
phrases.english: Because the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not rejoice
over the downfall of the wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי חָדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּמַפַּלְתָּן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of 'כן ישיש' in רבי יהושע בן לוי's פתיחתא
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 38 that ה׳ will 'rejoice' to bring harm on the wicked
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן shows from the missing 'כי טוב' that ה׳ does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, so a פסוק saying He rejoices seems to contradict this.

steps.title: The angels were not allowed to sing at the sea
steps.stepSummary: A second teaching of רבי יוחנן: when the Egyptians drowned, ה׳ stopped the angels from singing, because His creations were dying.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן also explained the פסוק 'and one did not come near the other all night': the angels wanted to sing, but ה׳ said, 'My creations are drowning in the sea, and you want to sing?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds more support to its challenge. A second teaching of רבי יוחנן shows again that ה׳ does not rejoice when the wicked are destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The angels normally sing by calling 'one to another.' The פסוק says 'one did not come near the other all night,' which means the angels did not sing together that night. ה׳ stopped them because the Egyptians, even though they were wicked, are still 'the work of My hands.'

keyTerms.meaning: The work of My hands, My creations

phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן said: What is the meaning of what is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״וְלֹא קָרַב זֶה אֶל זֶה כׇּל הַלָּיְלָה״ —
phrases.english: "And one did not come near the other all the night"?
phrases.notes: The גמרא reads 'one to the other' as the angels, who usually call out to each other when they sing.

phrases.english: The ministering angels wanted to say song,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
The work of My hands is drowning in the sea,
phrases.notes: He means the Egyptians.

phrases.english: and you are saying song?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source that makes the challenge of step 39 stronger
steps.raayaObject: That ה׳ does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 14:20, 'ולא קרב זה אל זה כל הלילה', as explained by רבי יוחנן

steps.title: ה׳ does not rejoice, but He makes others rejoice
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers: ה׳ Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: He Himself does not rejoice, but He makes others rejoice.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the challenge. Both ideas are true: ה׳ is not happy Himself, but He makes others happy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's teachings are about ה׳'s own feeling, so He does not rejoice. The פסוק in דברים is about what ה׳ causes, so He brings joy to others, like the people who are saved. So there is no contradiction.

phrases.english: רבי אלעזר said:
He Himself does not rejoice,
but He causes others to rejoice.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: הוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מֵשִׂישׂ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 39-40
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: ה׳'s own joy versus joy He causes others
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'כן ישיש' means ה׳ Himself rejoices at harming the wicked
steps.terutzMaskana: 'כן ישיש' means ה׳ causes others to rejoice, while He Himself does not

steps.title: The spelling 'ישיש' proves the answer
steps.stepSummary: The wording of the פסוק supports רבי אלעזר: it says 'ישיש' (causes rejoicing), not 'ישוש' (rejoices).
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording shows this too, since it is written 'כן ישיש' and not 'ישוש.' Learn from it that this is right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבי אלעזר's answer from the exact word in the פסוק, and then accepts it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ישוש' would mean 'He will rejoice.' The form 'ישיש' can mean 'He will make others rejoice.' Because the פסוק uses 'ישיש,' it fits רבי אלעזר's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is also precise in the wording; the text supports this
Learn from it; this is proven

steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ does not rejoice when the wicked fall, since they are still His creations. But He brings joy to others, the people who are saved. That is how פורים joy fits with this idea.

phrases.english: And it is precise as well, as it is written: "So He will cause to rejoice [yasis],"
and it is not written "yasus."
phrases.notes: 'Yasus' would simply mean 'He will rejoice,' so the different form points to making others happy.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדַיְקָא נָמֵי, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אלעזר's answer from the wording of the פסוק
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's distinction that ה׳ causes others to rejoice
steps.raayaSupportSource: The spelling 'ישיש' instead of 'ישוש' in דברים 28:63

steps.title: A new opening: the sinner gathers for the righteous
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר כהנא opens the מגילה with a פסוק from קהלת: the good man is מרדכי, the sinner who gathers is המן, and what המן gathered was given to מרדכי and אסתר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר כהנא opened this section from here: 'To a man who is good before Him, He gave wisdom, knowledge, and joy' means מרדכי. 'And to the sinner He gave the task of gathering and collecting' means המן. 'To give it to the one who is good before God' means מרדכי and אסתר, as it says: 'And אסתר set מרדכי over the house of המן.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new פתיחתא, a new introduction to the מגילה. Each part of a פסוק in קהלת is matched to a person in the story of פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: המן worked hard to collect wealth and power, but in the end everything he gathered went to the righteous. The proof is that אסתר put מרדכי in charge of המן's house. The פסוק sums up the whole turnaround of the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Opened with an introduction (a פתיחתא) to the topic

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא
phrases.english: רבי אבא בר כהנא opened an introduction
to this section from here:
"To a man who is good before Him,
phrases.notes: This פסוק is from קהלת.

phrases.english: He gave wisdom and knowledge and joy" —
this is מרדכי the righteous;
"and to the sinner He gave the task of gathering and collecting" —
this is המן;
"to give to the one who is good before God" —
this is מרדכי and אסתר,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״וַתָּשֶׂם אֶסְתֵּר אֶת מׇרְדֳּכַי עַל בֵּית הָמָן״.
phrases.english: as it is written: "And אסתר set מרדכי over the house of המן."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new פתיחתא after the discussion of רבי יהושע בן לוי's opening is resolved
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קהלת 2:26 describes the מגילה: what the sinner המן gathered was given to the righteous מרדכי and אסתר.

steps.title: רבה בר עופרן's opening: the king and princes destroyed in עילם
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר עופרן opens the מגילה with a פסוק from ירמיהו. The 'king' who is destroyed is ושתי, and the 'princes' are המן and his ten sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר עופרן opened this section with this פסוק: 'And I will set My throne in Elam, and destroy from there the king and the princes.' 'King' means ושתי. 'Princes' means המן and his ten sons.
steps.whatsHappening: This is another opening teaching for the מגילה, like רבי אבא בר כהנא's in step 43. רבה בר עופרן shows that a פסוק in ירמיהו hints to the פורים story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks about ה׳ placing His throne in עילם, the land where שושן was. It names two groups who get destroyed, and the גמרא matches each to the מגילה: ושתי, who was removed, and המן with his sons, who were hanged. The message is that ה׳ was quietly in control in the Persian kingdom.

keyTerms.meaning: He opened with an opening, meaning he introduced the topic with a פסוק from elsewhere
Section or passage. Here it means the מגילה
Elam, the region of Persia where שושן was
And his ten sons, the sons of המן who were hanged

steps.confusionAlert: Don't be thrown by ושתי being called 'king.' The פסוק simply says 'king,' and the גמרא applies that word to ושתי, the royal figure who was removed.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר עוֹפְרָן פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא
phrases.english: Rabba bar Oferan opened with an introduction
to this section, from here:
phrases.notes: 'This section' means מגילת אסתר.

phrases.english: "And I will set My throne in Elam
phrases.notes: This is a פסוק in ירמיהו. שושן, the city of the Purim story, was in Elam.

phrases.english: and I will destroy from there king and princes."
"King": this is Vashti,
"and princes": this is Haman and his ten sons.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר עוֹפְרָן פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a parallel opening teaching for the מגילה, added after רבי אבא בר כהנא's opening in step 43.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק 'I will destroy from there king and princes' hints to the downfall of ושתי and of המן with his ten sons.

steps.title: Introducing רב דימי בר יצחק's opening
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins the next opening teaching, by רב דימי בר יצחק. His פסוק appears in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי בר יצחק opened this section with this פסוק:
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next opening teaching. It names רב דימי בר יצחק, and the פסוק he uses comes right on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same formula used for the earlier openings. It only tells us who is speaking next. Nothing has been taught yet, so wait for the פסוק in the next part of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: From here, introducing the פסוק that will be quoted
The אמורא who gives the next opening teaching

phrases.aramaic: רַב דִּימִי בַּר יִצְחָק פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא
phrases.english: Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak opened with an introduction
to this section, from here:

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב דִּימִי בַּר יִצְחָק פָּתַח לַהּ פִּיתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרַשְׁתָּא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the setup line for the next opening teaching in the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This line only introduces רב דימי בר יצחק's opening. Its content follows on the next amud.
